'''Harvey Douglas Keith''' (10 March 1927&nbsp;– 9 February 2003) was a British [[physicist]] and one of the primary [[polymer]] researchers over the latter half of the 20th century.<ref name=Macromolecules>{{cite journal|last1=Lovinger|first1=Andrew J.|last2=Bates|first2=Frank S.|last3=Cheng|first3=Stephen Z.D.|author-link3=Stephen Z.D. Cheng|last4=Khoury|first4=Freddy A.|last5=Koberstein |first5=Jeffrey T.|last6=Lotz|first6=Bernard|last7=Russell|first7=Thomas P.|last8=Thomas|first8=Edwin L.|date=30 August 2002|title=H. Douglas Keith – Tribute|journal=[[Macromolecules (journal)|Macromolecules]]|volume=35|issue=20|pages=7527–7528|doi=10.1021/ma0211737|quote=...the 'Keith and Padden theory of spherulitic crystallization' … explained the crystallization and structure of polymeric spherulites based upon competition between their crystalline growth rate and diffusional processes in the melt and has been used very extensively in the study of polymer melt solidification}}</ref><ref name=PhysicsToday>{{cite journal|last1=Bates|first1=Frank S.|last2=Cheng|first2=Stephen Z.D.|author-link2=Stephen Z.D. Cheng|last3=Lovinger|first3=Andrew J.|date=April 2004|title=Obituaries: H. Douglas Keith|journal=Physics Today|volume=57|issue=4|page=106|doi=10.1063/1.1752439|df=dmy-all|doi-access=}}</ref>

==Early UK University affiliations==
In 1948, Keith obtained a BSc degree from [[Queen's University Belfast|Queen's University in Belfast]]. In 1951, he received a PhD in physics from the [[University of Bristol]] in England, where he taught [[optics]] as a lecturer in Physics between 1951 and 1956.<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday />

==Industrial career==
Keith immigrated to the United States in 1956 after accepting a position at the [[American Viscose Corporation]] in [[Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania]], where he began researching the complex structures and morphologies of [[macromolecule]]s. There, he met his lifelong collaborator, Frank J. Padden Jr. Together, they began to examine the optical properties of [[spherulite]]s from both theoretical and experimental approaches ''(see [[Spherulite (polymer physics)|Spherulite]])''.<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday />

Keith and Padden joined [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]] in [[Murray Hill, New Jersey|Murray Hill, NJ]] in 1960. Not long after they arrived, they published a seminal paper on spherulitic [[crystallisation]].<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday /> They subsequently studied the [[Crystal structure|crystalline structures]] of isotactic [[polypropylene]], isotactic [[polystyrene]], [[polyester]]s, various polypeptides (''see [[Peptide]]''), and other crystallisable [[polymer]]s. In 1965, Keith and his collaborators explained the mechanical strength of polymers by discovering their intercrystalline links.<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday />

A team led by Keith led, including Padden, Lotz and Giannoni, produced the first chain-folded single DNA crystals in 1969.<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday /> For this and their later work, the American Physical Society awarded its Polymer Physics Prize to Keith & Padden in 1973.<ref name=APS>{{cite web|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?name=H.%20Douglas%20Keith%20and%20Frank%20J.%20Padden%2C%20Jr.&year=1973|title=1973 Polymer Physics Prize Recipient|publisher=American Physical Society|location=College Park, MD|access-date=25 September 2010}}</ref>

Later, he was named Head of the Analytical Chemistry Research Department at AT&T Bell Laboratories. He subsequently became Head of the Organic Materials Research Department.<ref name=Macromolecules />

==The Keith and Padden theory==
Forming the basis of what has become known as the Keith and Padden theory, the two researchers published "Twisting orientation and the role of transient states in polymer crystallization"<ref name=Polymer>{{cite journal|last1=Keith|first1=H.D.|author-link=H. Douglas Keith|last2=Padden|first2=F. J. Jr.|date=January 1984|title=Twisting orientation and the role of transient states in polymer crystallization|journal=Polymer|volume=25|issue=1|pages=28–42|doi=10.1016/0032-3861(84)90264-7}}</ref> in 1984 and "Banding in Polyethylene and other spherulites"<ref name="Macromolecules2">{{cite journal|last1=Keith|first1=H.D.|author-link=H. Douglas Keith|last2=Padden|first2=F.J. Jr.|year=1996|title=Banding in Polyethylene and Other Spherulites|journal=[[Macromolecules (journal)|Macromolecules]]|volume=29|issue=24|pages=7776–7786|doi=10.1021/ma960634j|bibcode=1996MaMol..29.7776K}}</ref> in 1996. These two papers addressed the long-standing problem of accounting for the origins of [[lamellar]] (a thin layer) twisting in banded polymer spherulites. The Keith and Padden theory posits that a lamella twists because each of its two halves tend to scroll in opposite directions. Their theory asserts that rather than twisting, one of the lamella's halves will shrink or waste away. This leads to a scrolled appearance instead of seeming twisted.<ref name="Macromolecules3">{{cite journal|last1=Maillard|first1=Damien|last2=Prud'homme|first2=Robert E.|date=8 February 2008|title=Crystallization of Ultrathin Films of Polylactides: From Chain Chirality to Lamella Curvature and Twisting|journal=[[Macromolecules (journal)|Macromolecules]]|volume=41|issue=5|pages=1705–1712|doi=10.1021/ma071306u|bibcode=2008MaMol..41.1705M}}</ref>

==Later academic research==
After his retirement from Bell Labs in 1988, Keith continued his polymer morphology research as a faculty member at the [[University of Connecticut]]. He became a [[Professor Emeritus]] in 1996.<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday />

==Affiliations/honours==
Keith was active as a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society|American Physical Society (APS)]]. In 1965–1966, he chaired the Polymer Physics Division, and in 1977–1985 served as the Divisional Councilor at the APS Council. He was a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)]].

In 1986, he was the Fraser Price Lecturer at the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]]. He served on the Editorial Advisory Boards of two research journals, [[Macromolecules (journal)|Macromolecules]] and the [[Journal of Polymer Science Part B]].<ref name=Macromolecules /><ref name=PhysicsToday />

==Death==
On 9 February 2003, Keith died from cancer at his home in [[South Windsor, Connecticut]], aged 75.<ref name=PhysicsToday />
